CVS Health stock faces 2028 split into two public companies
sum: CVS Health announced on Wednesday, November 4, that it intends to separate its healthcare solutions and retail pharmacy operations into two independent, publicly traded companies. The plan adds a major strategic development to the company's third-quarter results and higher full-year 2026 guidance.

According to the SEC filing, the healthcare solutions company will comprise Aetna, CVS Caremark, CVS Specialty, Oak Street Health and Signify Health. The retail business, which will be named CVS Pharmacy, will include approximately 9,000 pharmacies, mail pharmacy, MinuteClinic and Health100.

The separation is expected to be completed in the first half of 2028. It is intended to be tax-free to CVS Health and its shareholders, but remains subject to customary conditions, including board approval, an effective registration statement and tax-related confirmation.

Upon completion, CVS Health shareholders are expected to own shares in both companies. David Joyner is slated to lead the healthcare solutions company, while Prem Shah is slated to become chief executive of CVS Pharmacy. The planned structure is intended to give each business a more focused strategy and capital structure.

The filing also said CVS Health announced third-quarter 2026 results and raised its full-year guidance on the same day. That earnings update gives investors a second operating theme to weigh alongside the proposed separation, while the transaction itself remains a forward-looking plan.

CVS Announces Split Into Two: Pharmacy and Insurance to Separate, Shares Plunge More Than 12% in a Single Day
sum: U.S. healthcare giant CVS Health (CVS) announced a major organizational restructuring on Wednesday (November 4), planning to split the group into two independent publicly traded companies, one focused on retail pharmacy and the other on insurance and medical services. The news was not met with market applause, as CVS shares plunged about 12.5% that day, reflecting investor concerns over the lack of detail on the separation.

Under the plan, the company retaining the CVS Health name will continue to be led by current Chief Executive Officer David Joyner, with operations spanning Aetna health insurance, CVS Caremark pharmacy benefit management (PBM), the CVS Specialty business, and medical services businesses including Oak Street Health and Signify Health. The other independent company will be named CVS Pharmacy, with current group President Prem Shah serving as CEO, encompassing roughly 9,000 physical pharmacies, mail-order pharmacy, MinuteClinic retail clinics, and the Health100 technology services platform.

The separation is expected to be completed in the first half of 2028 and remains subject to regulatory approvals. CVS emphasized that existing customers' prescription drugs, medical services and insurance benefits will not be immediately affected; upon completion of the separation, existing shareholders will hold shares in both companies, and the transaction is structured to be tax-free.

Explaining the decision, Joyner said that over the past two years, operations at the company's 9,000 pharmacies, Caremark and Aetna had all improved markedly, which gave the company the conditions to undertake the organizational restructuring. He noted that the pharmacy side boosted throughput by upgrading store technology and adjusted its prescription reimbursement model so that it can offer lower prices while still maintaining margins on branded and generic drugs. He also said bluntly in an interview: "Every business is executing very well, and we now have the room to make different decisions that I couldn't have made two years ago."
Paradoxically, the third-quarter results CVS reported the same day were not bad at all.

sum: Despite beating third-quarter revenue and earnings expectations, CVS Health shares tumbled 12.5% following its plan to split into two independent publicly traded companies by the first half of 2028. Investors remain anxious due to vague financial details regarding debt allocation, separation costs, and the loss of vertical integration synergies. Furthermore, persistent regulatory scrutiny, rising medical costs, and structural headwinds in the retail pharmacy segment weigh on the outlook. Technistically, the stock has broken key support levels, indicating strong downside momentum with critical support at $78.25, though nearing oversold RSI conditions suggest potential for near-term consolidation.

TradingKey - CVS Health (CVS) delivered an eighth consecutive quarter of results that topped market expectations, yet failed to win over investors. On November 4, the company announced plans to split its business into two independent publicly traded companies in the first half of 2028. Following the announcement, its shares plunged 12.5% to near six-month lows. Although both third-quarter revenue and adjusted earnings per share exceeded Wall Street estimates and the company raised its future earnings guidance, investors remain skeptical about the breakup plan's lack of concrete financial arrangements, the potential loss of synergies, and ongoing regulatory pressures.

Judging from its third-quarter earnings report, CVS's operational performance was actually quite solid. The company generated revenue of $108.4 billion, up about 5% year-over-year and above analyst expectations of $104.8 billion. Adjusted earnings per share reached $2.09, significantly topping market estimates of $1.65. Its medical benefit ratio (MLR), a measure of medical cost pressure in the insurance business, stood at 91.3%, below the market consensus of 92.3%. A lower ratio typically indicates that medical costs account for a smaller proportion of premium revenue, which is favorable for profitability. In addition, the company expects adjusted EPS to reach at least $8.65 in 2027, also exceeding Wall Street's average estimate of roughly $8.53.
However, the positive signals in the earnings report did not alleviate market concerns regarding the company's long-term business model.

sum: CVS Health is due to release third-quarter 2026 results before US markets open on Wednesday, November 4. The report will test whether improving insurance economics can offset pressure in pharmacy services and medical costs.

In its earnings preview published October 26, Zacks Investment Research projected third-quarter adjusted earnings of USD 1.62 per share and revenue of USD 105.04 billion. The estimates imply modest year-over-year growth, while Zacks said the forecast had remained unchanged over the previous 60 days.

Zacks expects Aetna's margin recovery and strength in the Government business to support Health Care Benefits. Elevated medical-cost utilization and the company's exit from the individual exchange business remain potential offsets.

Health Services may benefit from pharmacy drug mix, purchasing economics and growth at Oak Street Health. The Caremark pharmacy benefit manager still faces pressure in its 340B business, where program changes and contract dynamics could weigh on performance.

Pharmacy and Consumer Wellness may receive support from prescription volume, brand inflation and the Rite Aid transaction. Regulatory price reductions, generic-drug introductions and reimbursement pressure could limit the benefit.

Management's comments on fourth-quarter guidance, cost reduction, capital allocation and 2027 priorities may influence investors' assessment of the earnings quality. Zacks also highlighted CVS Health's technology investment and digital initiatives, while warning that 340B-related pressure could remain a near-term headwind.

CVS Settles DOJ Opioid Case for $315 Million: Here’s What It Means for the Stock
sum: CVS Health (CVS) agreed on Tuesday, October 13, to pay $315 million to settle a Justice Department lawsuit over opioid prescriptions, Reuters reported. The government alleged that CVS pharmacies filled invalid prescriptions for opioids and other controlled substances from October 2013 through December 2025, then billed Medicare and other federal programs for many of them. CVS didn’t admit wrongdoing and says it disagrees with the claims.
The stock barely noticed. CVS closed at $87.55 on Tuesday, down 0.2%, and was flat before Wednesday’s open.
- $315 million to resolve claims under the Controlled Substances Act and the False Claims Act
- A hotline for employees and the public to report suspicious prescriptions, plus monitoring of dispensing patterns (AP)
- No admission of liability (the case began as a former employee’s whistleblower suit, and the government filed its own complaint in December 2024)

CVS generated $10.64 billion of cash from operations in 2025 and has guided to at least $11.5 billion this year. The settlement is under 3% of either figure, or about 25 cents a share against an $88 stock.

It’s also the second federal case CVS has closed since July. CVS and Omnicare, its long-term care pharmacy unit, agreed to settle for at least $440 million against a judgment of nearly $950 million. CVS pays $130 million within two weeks of the agreement taking effect and covers any shortfall in a further $310 million if Omnicare’s estate hasn’t paid it by March 2028. Together, the two settlements come to about $755 million, roughly 7% of last year’s operating cash flow. Walmart (WMT) settled its own DOJ opioid-dispensing case for $50 million in August.

CVS vs. UNH: Which Health Insurance Stock Has More Upside Now?
sum: CVS Health CVS and UnitedHealth Group UNH, both S&P 500 companies, are two of the biggest players in the U.S. health insurance industry. CVS competes through its Aetna subsidiary, acquired in 2018, offering a broad range of products and related services, including medical, pharmacy, dental and behavioral health plans, medical management capabilities, and Medicare Advantage and Medicare Supplement plans. The company also operates Health Services, Pharmacy & Consumer Wellness and Corporate/Other segments.

UnitedHealth, on the other hand, sells a broad range of health benefits through UnitedHealthcare, serving individuals and employers, seniors and other Medicare-eligible consumers, as well as economically disadvantaged and medically underserved populations. The company also has an information and technology-enabled health services business called Optum, comprising Optum Health, Optum Insight and Optum Rx. The divisions combine capabilities in value-based care, population health, health care operations, data and analytics and pharmacy care services.
Over the past six months, CVS and UNH shares have risen 13.9% and 33.2%, respectively, both outperforming the S&P 500 composite's 11.9% growth.
Let's take a closer look at which stock has the stronger investment case today.

CVS Health is implementing technology infrastructure changes to modernize its platforms and accelerate data sharing and connectivity with providers and payer partners. The company has committed to invest $20 billion over the next decade to transform the health care experience through emerging technologies, with a focus on building a more consumer-based health care technology business.

Aetna's margin recovery is becoming an important part of CVS' long-term growth story. Efforts around strengthening clinical programs, cost management, pricing and other operating improvements have driven more than $2 billion of year-over-year improvement in adjusted operating income so far in 2026. Management raised Health Care Benefits' adjusted operating income outlook to $5.03-$5.37 billion for 2026, more than $1 billion above its previous guidance.

items.t: Is CVS Stock a Buy as Earnings Improve but Key Risks Remain Elevated?
sum: CVS Health CVS is entering the second half of 2026 with stronger earnings momentum, higher cash generation and an improved Aetna profit outlook. Those gains strengthen the recovery case after a difficult period for the insurer.

The trade-off is that medical-cost pressure and changing pharmacy benefit manager economics remain unresolved. CVS trades below major valuation benchmarks, but its multiple is already above its own five-year median.

The Zacks Consensus Estimate for 2026 earnings has increased 7.9% over the prior four weeks, while projected 2026 EPS growth stands at 16.6%. Current cash flow growth of 65.3% adds another positive signal.

Second-quarter results support that trend. Adjusted EPS increased 42.5% year over year to $2.58, while adjusted operating income rose 35.4% to $5.16 billion. CVS also raised 2026 adjusted EPS guidance to $7.90-$8.10.

CVS trades at 11.7X forward 12-month earnings, below the Zacks sub-industry's 16.2X and the S&P 500's 20.8X. The gap shows that investors still assign CVS a sizable discount despite improving earnings.

The stock is less cheap against its own history. CVS' five-year median forward multiple is 10.3X, below the current level. Relative valuation is favorable, but the shares are not unusually inexpensive compared with their historical norm.

Health Care Benefits is the clearest operating reason for greater confidence. Adjusted operating income increased by more than $2 billion year over year in the first half of 2026 as pricing discipline and medical-cost management improved profitability.

sum: Investing.com -- CVS Health shares jumped about 5% in premarket trading Wednesday after the company raised its full-year profit guidance following better-than-expected second-quarter results.
